scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

I can’t make purchasing decisions for you, but I can certainly help you weigh the pros and cons of buying matching fabric for a family wedding! Here’s a balanced perspective to consider: ### **Potential Benefits:** 1. **Unity & Tradition** – If the wedding has a strong family tradition of coordinated outfits (e.g., bridesmaids, groomsmen, or even extended family), it can feel meaningful and symbolic. 2. **Photography** – Matching fabrics can create cohesive, visually striking photos, especially if everyone is wearing complementary colors or patterns. 3. **Ease of Coordination** – If you’re not great at matching outfits, this ensures everyone looks intentional and put-together. 4. **Sentimental Value** – Some families cherish the idea of "matching" as a way to honor the couple or create a shared memory. ### **Potential Drawbacks:** 1. **Cost** – Buying fabric (especially high-quality or custom-made) can be expensive, especially if multiple people are involved. Sewing or altering clothes may also add to the expense. 2. **Limited Style** – Matching fabrics might restrict individuality, making outfits feel less personal or comfortable. 3. **Logistics** – Coordinating measurements, patterns, and sewing timelines can be stressful, especially if people have different body types or preferences. 4. **Wearability** – If the fabric is formal (e.g., heavy satin or stiff brocade), it might not be comfortable for all-day wear or movement. 5. **Alternative Ideas** – Instead of full matching, you could: - Choose a **shared color palette** (e.g., everyone wears a shade of blue or gold). - Opt for **similar silhouettes** (e.g., all dresses with the same neckline or pants with matching details). - Use **accessories** (e.g., coordinated scarves, shoes, or jewelry) for a subtle touch. ### **Questions to Ask Yourself:** - **Is this a family expectation or tradition?** If it’s deeply meaningful, it might be worth it. - **How much flexibility do you have in styling?** Could you mix fabrics or patterns in a way that feels intentional? - **What’s the budget?** Could you compromise (e.g., matching shoes or bags instead of full outfits)? - **How do you feel about uniformity vs. individuality?** Would you prefer to stand out or blend in? ### **Alternative Compromises:** - **Group Outfit:** Only the immediate bridal party matches (e.g., bridesmaids + groomsmen in coordinated pieces). - **Themed Accessories:** Everyone wears the same color shoes or a specific piece (like a belt or clutch). - **Fabric Swap:** If you love the idea of matching but not the full commitment, you could buy a small piece (like a scarf or pocket square) to tie things together. Would you like help brainstorming specific outfit ideas based on the wedding’s theme or your personal style? Or would you prefer tips on negotiating the expectation with your family?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a **complicated but deeply valid** situation, and your feelings of guilt are completely understandable—especially given your family’s history and your love for your dad. **I don’t think you’re "wrong" for prioritizing your well-being here, but I also recognize why you’re torn.** Let’s break it down: ### **Why This Might Be Okay (or Even Necessary) for You:** 1. **Your Safety and Peace of Mind** - You’ve done the hard work of recognizing your sister’s emotional abuse and setting boundaries. Skipping the joint party to avoid her presence isn’t selfish—it’s **self-preservation**. Living with chronic anxiety around her is a form of ongoing trauma, and reducing exposure is a healthy step. - Therapy has helped you realize you’re not responsible for her behavior, which is a **huge** insight. This isn’t about "giving up" on her; it’s about protecting your own mental health. 2. **The Guilt Isn’t Yours to Carry Alone** - Your parents’ reaction might hurt, but **you’re not obligated to make them comfortable at the expense of your own well-being**. They’ve been pleading with you not to "give up" on her, but you’ve already done the work of setting boundaries. This is about **what works for you now**. - If they’re hurt, that’s their emotional labor to process—not yours. You’ve already had the conversation; this is just another layer of it. 3. **A Small, Strategic Compromise** - You’re not entirely avoiding your sister—you’re **choosing a time when you won’t have to endure her presence**. Leaving a gift is a thoughtful gesture that acknowledges her without requiring your energy. - This isn’t about "winning" or "losing"; it’s about **prioritizing your nervous system’s needs** in a situation where you can’t control her reactions. 4. **Your Dad’s Feelings Matter, But So Do Yours** - You’re right to worry about hurting him, but **he also knows about the abuse**. If he truly loves you, he’ll understand that your healing isn’t optional. If he can’t, that’s a separate issue to address later. - You could frame it gently: *"I know this weekend is important to you, and I wanted to be here for you. I’ll make sure to call you later to celebrate!"* This validates his feelings while still honoring your limits. --- ### **Why You Might Still Feel Guilty (And Why That’s Normal):** 1. **Family Loyalty and Love Language** - You’re deeply connected to your family, and **skipping a joint event might feel like betrayal** because it’s tied to love and tradition. But your love for them doesn’t mean you have to endure harm. - Guilt often stems from **internalized shame** about needing boundaries. Remind yourself: *This isn’t about rejecting them; it’s about reclaiming your life.* 2. **Fear of Escalation** - If your sister is volatile, you might worry that skipping will "provoke" her. But **you’re not the one causing her distress—she’s the one who creates it**. Your absence isn’t a rejection of her; it’s a refusal to be her punching bag. 3. **The "What If" Trap** - *"What if I never see her again?"* or *"What if this makes things worse?"* These fears are valid, but **you’re not making a permanent decision here**. This is a **tactical choice** to protect yourself in the moment. --- ### **How to Move Forward with Less Guilt:** 1. **Reframe the Narrative** - Instead of *"I’m skipping to avoid her,"* think: *"I’m choosing to celebrate my dad in a way that doesn’t drain me."* - You’re not "choosing her over him"—you’re **choosing yourself so you can show up fully for him later**. 2. **Prepare for Their Reaction** - If they’re upset, you can say: *"I know this might feel like I’m avoiding her, but I’ve been doing a lot of work on my mental health, and I need to set boundaries that protect me. I love you both, and I want to be the best version of myself for you."* - This sets a firm but kind boundary while keeping the door open for future conversations. 3. **Give Yourself Permission** - You’ve already done the hard work of recognizing the abuse and seeking help. **This is just another step in that process.** It’s okay to prioritize your healing. 4. **Consider a "Gray Area" Compromise** - If you feel too guilty about skipping entirely, could you: - Attend the party **briefly** (e.g., arrive late, leave early) to show support for your dad? - Celebrate your dad **separately** in a way that feels safe (e.g., a small gathering with just him and your husband)? --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (You’re Not Wrong)** This isn’t about being a "bad daughter" or "selfish." It’s about **honoring your truth while still loving your family from a place of wholeness**. You’re not obligated to endure emotional harm for anyone’s comfort—especially not your own. Your parents’ reaction will teach you a lot about where they’re at in their understanding. If they can’t accept your boundaries, that’s their issue to work through. **You’ve already done the hardest part: recognizing the abuse and deciding what you’ll tolerate. This is just another layer of that.** --- **TL;DR:** You’re not wrong for prioritizing your well-being. This is a healthy, necessary step in your healing journey. The guilt will fade as you remind yourself that your peace matters too.
